steps.body: How far to move the point is set by the DIVISOR: shift it just far enough to make the divisor whole, then shift the dividend the same way.
steps.narration: How far to move the point is set by the DIVISOR: shift it just far enough to make the divisor whole, then shift the dividend the same way.

widget.prompt: 3.5 ÷ 0.07 — slide to the quotient after shifting both two places.
widget.lowFeedback: Too low — sevenths of a hundredth are tiny, so a great many of them fit inside 3.5.
widget.highFeedback: Too high — 350 ÷ 7 is fifty, not the hundreds.
widget.successFeedback: 50 — two shifts turn 3.5 ÷ 0.07 into 350 ÷ 7, and the quotient is unchanged at 50.

predict.prompt: Dividing by 0.07, how many places must the point move?
predict.reveal: 0.07 needs two shifts to become the whole number 7, and the dividend must move two as well.

cml.actionGoal: Work in the smallest place the numbers use, then decide where the point belongs for g5dc shift.
invariants: A decimal is place value continued past the ones: computing in the smallest shared place turns g5dc shift into whole-number arithmetic, and the point's position records which place the digits landed in.
misconceptions: Right-aligning digits instead of the points, treating a trailing zero as a change in value, or losing count of the decimal places a product carries.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the point moved one place left, how many times smaller would the amount become?

widget.prompt: To compute 7.2 ÷ 0.9, why multiply BOTH numbers by 10 first?

options.label: Because scaling both by the same factor leaves the quotient unchanged
options.feedback: Correct — 72 ÷ 9 has the same answer as 7.2 ÷ 0.9, and a whole-number divisor is far easier to work with.

options.label: Because it makes the answer ten times bigger
options.feedback: It does not change the answer at all — that is precisely why the move is legal.

options.label: Because you may only divide whole numbers
options.feedback: Dividing by a decimal is perfectly valid; scaling is a convenience, not a requirement.

options.label: Because 0.9 rounds to 1
options.feedback: Rounding would change the answer; scaling both numbers preserves it exactly.

widget.prompt: Computing 0.4 × 0.3 in hundredths gives 12. Where does the point go?

options.label: 0.12 — one decimal place from each factor makes two in the product
options.feedback: Correct — tenths times tenths gives hundredths, so the product carries two decimal places.

options.label: 1.2 — one decimal place
options.feedback: That counts only one factor's place. Each factor contributes its own, so the product has two.

options.label: 12 — no decimal places
options.feedback: Multiplying two numbers below one cannot produce twelve; the product must be smaller than either factor.

options.label: 0.012 — three decimal places
options.feedback: Three places would need a thousandth somewhere; one tenth times one tenth reaches only hundredths.
